readingInstruction: Read Acts 23:1-24:27. Paul appears before the Sanhedrin, the Lord encourages him, a plot is foiled, and he is brought to Caesarea to stand before Governor Felix. Notice Paul’s conscience and the center of his defense: the resurrection.
settingTheScene: Paul is in Roman custody, and the tribune brings him before the Jewish council to find out what he is accused of. Here and in the following hearings, Paul consistently turns the discussion to the hope of the resurrection. A plot of more than forty men to kill him is uncovered by his nephew, and he is moved by night to Caesarea, the Roman capital, where he is held under Governor Felix for two years.
observation: “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day” (23:1).
“Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial” (23:6).
“The following night the Lord stood by him and said, Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome” (23:11).
“According to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets” (24:14).
“Having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust” (24:15).
“So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man” (24:16).
“And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and future judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you” (24:25).
interpretation:
Before the council, Paul begins, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” The high priest Ananias orders him struck on the mouth. Paul says, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall!” When told that he is speaking to the high priest, Paul apologizes, acknowledging the law: “You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.” Even apostles had sharp moments.

Then Paul realizes the council is divided between Sadducees and Pharisees. He cries out, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” The council erupts in dispute. Some argue that they find nothing wrong with the man. The tribune, fearing Paul will be torn to pieces, takes him back to the barracks. That night, “the Lord stood by him and said, Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” This is a vital promise. Whatever happens, Paul will reach Rome.

A plot is hatched: more than forty men take an oath neither to eat nor drink until they have killed Paul. Paul’s nephew hears of it and warns the tribune, who sends Paul under heavy guard (two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, two hundred spearmen) to Governor Felix in Caesarea. God uses the Roman army to protect his apostle.

Five days later, the high priest and a lawyer named Tertullus arrive and accuse Paul. Paul’s defense is calm and clear. He had not stirred up a crowd; he came to Jerusalem to bring alms. “According to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets.” The Christian faith is not a new religion but the fulfillment of Israel’s hope. His hope is the resurrection of both the just and the unjust. “So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man.”

Felix, who knows more about the Way than most, puts off a decision. Later, he and his wife Drusilla hear Paul speak about faith in Christ Jesus. As Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and future judgment, Felix becomes alarmed and sends him away. He hopes for a bribe and sends for Paul often, but nothing changes. After two years, Felix is succeeded by Festus, and desiring to do the Jews a favor, he leaves Paul in prison. Felix is a warning: he heard the truth, was alarmed, and put it off.
connection: Exodus 22:28 is the law Paul cites about speaking evil of rulers. Daniel 12:2 speaks of the resurrection of the just and the unjust. Luke 20:27-38 records Jesus on the resurrection against the Sadducees. Acts 4:1-2 and 17:32 show the resurrection as a point of dispute. 1 Corinthians 15 is Paul’s great chapter on the resurrection. 2 Corinthians 1:12 mentions a clear conscience. 1 Timothy 1:5 and 1:19 speak of a good conscience. Proverbs 27:1 warns against boasting about tomorrow. Hebrews 3:15 says today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.
application:
Ask whether your conscience is clear before God and man. If not, confess and make it right.

Do you put off a conviction because the timing is not convenient? Respond today.

Take courage from the Lord’s word to Paul. He stands by you too.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for standing by Paul, and ask him to stand by you.
Ask him for a clear conscience before him.
